explanations.answer: To come and heal his servant
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The centurion, an army officer, hears about Jesus and sends Jewish elders to ask Him to come and heal his servant (Luke 7:3). His servant is sick and about to die. I think when somebody you care about is that sick, you go to the One who can help.

explanations.answer: To come and bless his house
explanations.explanation: Ha! Nobody sends elders across town for that when someone's about to die, friend. The text says he sent them "…to ask Him to come and heal his servant." (Luke 7:3). His servant is sick and about to die, so I think the centurion skips the small talk and asks for the one thing that matters.

explanations.answer: To come and teach his soldiers
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd guess that, baker, since he's an officer with soldiers. But the elders aren't carrying a message about training anybody. The text says he sent them "…to ask Him to come and heal his servant." (Luke 7:3). His servant is sick and about to die, so healing is the request.

explanations.answer: He loves our nation and built our synagogue
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The elders say, "…he loves our nation and has built our synagogue." (Luke 7:5) Love for the people and a building to show for it. That's a reason you can point at, and the elders plead earnestly with Jesus about it (Luke 7:4).

explanations.answer: He feeds our poor and keeps the Sabbath
explanations.explanation: Nice list, friend, but the elders never read it out. What they tell Jesus is that the centurion "…loves our nation and has built our synagogue." (Luke 7:5). Built it! I've stamped a whole lot of cookies in my day and never built so much as a shelf.

explanations.answer: He fasts often and gives to the temple
explanations.explanation: That's a résumé the elders never hand over, baker. They say the centurion "…loves our nation and has built our synagogue." (Luke 7:5). He built a whole synagogue. The biggest thing I've ever built is a cookie box, and I needed a lot of help with that.

Not quite, friend. The centurion's message says, "Lord, do not trouble Yourself, for I am not worthy to have You come under my roof." (Luke 7:6) Nothing in it tells Jesus to hurry inside. He tells Jesus not to trouble Himself.

Right, baker. The centurion's message says, "Lord, do not trouble Yourself, for I am not worthy to have You come under my roof." (Luke 7:6) There's no "hurry inside" anywhere in it. He calls Jesus "Lord" and says he's not worthy to have Him come under his roof.

Yes, baker. He says, "But just say the word, and my servant will be healed." (Luke 7:7) No house call needed. He believes a word from Jesus is enough, and that's a whole lot of trust packed into one sentence.

explanations.answer: By sending one of His disciples
explanations.explanation: I see the thinking, friend, but the disciples never come up in his request. The centurion says, "But just say the word, and my servant will be healed." (Luke 7:7) He's asking Jesus Himself, and all he wants is a word from Him. No stand-in required.

Hold on, baker, nobody is rescheduling here. His servant is about to die (Luke 7:2), and the centurion asks Jesus to "…just say the word, and my servant will be healed." (Luke 7:7) The request is for a word, not for a later visit. Nothing in the text pushes it to another day.

Not this time, friend. Nobody's arguing in this speech. The centurion says, "I tell one to go, and he goes, and another to come, and he comes." (Luke 7:8) That's the picture he draws: an order given and an order done. No debate in sight.

That's right, baker. The centurion says, "I tell one to go, and he goes, and another to come, and he comes." (Luke 7:8) He says they go and they come, and he never mentions an argument. His whole point is that when the word is given, the thing happens.

You got it, baker. The text says, "When Jesus heard this, He marveled at the centurion." (Luke 7:9) Jesus heard those words about authority and was amazed. Then He turns to the crowd and says, "I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such great faith." (Luke 7:9)

Not a frown, friend. The text says Jesus "…marveled at the centurion." (Luke 7:9) Marveled means He was amazed, and the next thing He does is talk to the crowd about this man's faith. A frown doesn't fit that at all.

Close in sound, baker, but there's no sigh in the text. It says Jesus "…marveled at the centurion." (Luke 7:9) He was amazed by what the man said. Then He turns to the crowd and says, "I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such great faith." (Luke 7:9)

explanations.answer: He hasn't found faith this great even in Israel
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus turns to the crowd and says, "I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such great faith." (Luke 7:9) The man trusted that a word from Jesus was enough. The centurion is a Roman army officer, and Jesus says this in front of everyone.

explanations.answer: He has seen faith like this in every town
explanations.explanation: Other way around, friend. Jesus says, "I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such great faith." (Luke 7:9) He's saying He hasn't found it, even in Israel. That's what makes the centurion stand out.

explanations.answer: This faith still has to grow before the healing
explanations.explanation: Nope, baker, Jesus doesn't ask for a thing more. He calls it "…such great faith." and says He hasn't found it even in Israel (Luke 7:9). Nothing in His words says it needs to grow first. He just marvels at it.

Yes, baker. The text says, "…when the messengers returned to the house, they found the servant in good health." (Luke 7:10) The servant who was about to die is well. The centurion asked for a word, and when the messengers got home, there he was, healthy.

Not false, friend. The text says the messengers "…found the servant in good health." (Luke 7:10) This is the servant who was sick and about to die back in verse 2. The story ends with him well, and that's a good place to end.
